readerTitle: One-way doors, two-way doors: how to tell which decisions deserve your time
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Amazon, 2015년 주주서한의 Type 1·Type 2 결정) + 가상 적용 (마케팅 대행사, 가구 제조사)
insight: 결정에 쓸 시간은 결정의 크기가 아니라 '틀렸을 때 되돌리는 비용'으로 정하며, 되돌릴 수 없는 결정도 구조를 바꾸면 되돌릴 수 있게 만들 수 있다.
misconception: 중요한 결정일수록, 돈이 많이 걸릴수록 무조건 오래 신중하게 따져야 한다. 모든 결정에 같은 수준의 검토를 하는 것이 책임감 있는 태도다.

sources.text: Jeff Bezos, 2015 Letter to Amazon Shareholders (published April 2016): Type 1 and Type 2 decisions, one-way and two-way doors
대행사와 가구 제조사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Type 1/Type 2, 'one-way doors', 'two-way doors' 표현이 2015년 주주서한(2016년 4월 공개)에 나오는지 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드 3의 '조직이 커질수록 Type 2 결정에도 무거운 절차를 쓰는 경향이 생겨 느려지고 실험이 줄어든다'는 원문을 요약한 것이며 직접 인용이 아닙니다.
2016년 주주서한의 '정보 70%' 원칙은 THK-05-06(결정 속도)과 겹치므로 의도적으로 넣지 않았습니다.
가구 제조사 수치($400,000 기계, 3개월 외주 테스트)는 모두 가상입니다. 계산이 필요한 주장은 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: One-way doors, two-way doors
body: In his 2015 letter to shareholders, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos split decisions into two kinds. Some are like a door that locks behind you. Most are like a door you can walk back through.
His worry wasn't that people decided too fast. It was that they treated almost every door as if it locked.

image.label: Two doors, one with a lock, one swinging both ways
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 나란히 선 문 두 개. 왼쪽 문은 한쪽으로만 열리고 자물쇠와 '한 방향' 화살표, 오른쪽 문은 양쪽으로 흔들리는 스윙 도어와 양방향 화살표. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: Three decisions, one week.
body: You run a 20-person marketing agency. This week you must decide three things: a new price list for small clients, a new format for weekly team meetings, and a seven-year exclusive contract with your biggest client that bars you from working with its rivals.
Where do you spend your careful thinking?

options.text: Give all three the same thorough review
options.feedback: It feels responsible, but it slows the two easy calls and spreads your attention thin on the one that matters most.

options.text: Settle prices and meetings this week; take your time on the contract
options.feedback: Prices and meetings can be changed next month. A seven-year exclusive deal can't, so it gets the deep thinking.

options.text: Focus on the price list first, since it affects revenue most
options.feedback: Revenue impact matters, but a price list is easy to adjust. The contract is the harder one to undo.

cards.title: Type 1 and Type 2 decisions
body: Bezos called the locked-door kind **Type 1**: consequential and hard or impossible to undo. These deserve slow, careful thought and wide consultation.
**Type 2** decisions can be changed. If you get one wrong, you go back through the door and try again. These should be made quickly by small groups or individuals.
His warning: as companies grow, they start using the heavy Type 1 process on Type 2 decisions. The result is slowness, too little experimenting and less invention.

cards.title: Reversible vs irreversible decisions
body: A decision is **reversible** when you can undo it at a low cost. It is **irreversible** when undoing it is impossible or very expensive.
Notice what this is not. It is not about how big the decision feels. A large budget for a one-month test can be easy to reverse. A small promise to a key customer can be very hard to take back.
So the first question isn't "How important is this?" It's "If I'm wrong, what does it cost to undo?"

image.label: Two axes: size of decision vs cost to undo
image.brief: 2x2 매트릭스 인포그래픽. 가로축 'Size of decision', 세로축 'Cost to undo'. 오른쪽 아래 '큰 돈, 쉽게 되돌림(1개월 테스트)', 왼쪽 위 '작아 보여도 되돌리기 어려움(독점 계약)'. 위쪽 칸만 진한 색으로 강조.

cards.title: Mistakes run in both directions.
list: **Two-way door treated as one-way:** endless meetings, missed chances, nothing gets tested
**One-way door treated as two-way:** a rushed call you live with for years
cards.callout: Sort the door first. Then pick the speed.
cards.softwareNote: Changing a button, a pricing page or a feature behind an on/off switch is usually a two-way door. Deleting customer data, changing a public interface other companies build on, or migrating your whole database often isn't.

cards.title: You can often redesign the door.
body: Many decisions are only irreversible because of how they are set up. Change the setup, and the door swings both ways.
Rent before you buy. Hire on a trial project before a full-time offer. Launch in one city before ten. Sign a one-year deal with an option to extend instead of a five-year lock-in.
Each version costs a little more or moves a little slower. In return, you buy the right to change your mind.

image.label: A locked door being refitted with a swinging hinge
image.brief: 플랫 일러스트. 작업자가 자물쇠 달린 문의 경첩을 양방향 스윙 경첩으로 바꾸는 장면. 주변에 'Rent first', 'Pilot', 'Trial period' 라벨이 붙은 공구들.

cards.title: Some doors only look two-way.
body: Undoing has costs that don't show on a spreadsheet. Cut prices and customers may resist when you raise them back. Lay people off and trust doesn't return when you rehire. Break a promise to a client and the contract can be fixed, but the relationship may not be.
Flipping too often also has a price. A team that sees every decision reversed next week stops taking decisions seriously.
Before calling a door two-way, ask who else is affected if you walk back through it.

cards.title: Now it's a furniture factory.
body: You make wooden tables. A salesperson offers an automated cutting machine for $400,000. It could double output for a new line of office desks, but you haven't sold any desks yet.
What do you do?

options.text: Buy now, before the discount offer expires
options.feedback: You'd lock in a large, hard-to-resell asset based on demand you haven't seen. The discount is small next to that risk.

options.text: Pay a nearby shop with a similar machine to cut desks for three months, then decide
options.feedback: Each desk costs more to make for now. In exchange, you learn whether desks sell before walking through a one-way door.

options.text: Drop the desk idea; the machine is too risky
options.feedback: It avoids the big risk, but it also closes a cheap way to learn. The choice wasn't buy or nothing.

cards.title: Ask what it costs to undo before you ask how long to think.
body: Move fast through doors that swing both ways. Slow down at doors that lock. And when a door locks, look for a way to make it swing.
**Try it today:** list three decisions on your desk. Next to each, write how hard it would be to undo. Decide the easiest one before lunch.
